meta.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Classical and AI-Based Launch Adapter Ring Detection for Robotic On-Orbit Servicing
meta.authorsHtml: Kirimamuni Supuni Kaveendya<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Lina Maria Amaya-Mejia<sup>2</sup>, Miguel Olivares-Mendez<sup>3</sup>, Carol Martinez<sup>4</sup>

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: The Launch Adapter Ring (LAR) is a structural landmark that serves as a grasping interface and a distinct visual feature. Accurate and real-time detection of LAR is crucial for a successful robotic on-orbit servicing (OOS) mission. This paper conducts a comparative analysis of a classical computer vision (CV) approach vs a deep learning (DL)-based approach for LAR detection under varying lighting conditions and distance/scale changes. The classical approach relies on edge extraction and geometric ring detection, while the learning-based method employs a lightweight YOLOv8n convolutional neural network for real-time object detection. Detection accuracy and computational latency metrics are evaluated in both methods. The results demonstrate that the YOLOv8n detector provides higher robustness under illumination variations, while the classical method offers significantly lower computational costs, balancing between computational efficiency and detection accuracy.

blocks.html: On-orbit servicing (OOS) missions (e.g., refueling, repair, and assembly) have become the foundation of sustainable space operations. Having perception capabilities can enhance OOS operations by enabling object tracking, navigation in complex and dynamic environments, and improved precision, flexibility, and robustness.[1]. OOS missions are not like conventional missions. In these missions, the servicer spacecraft must approach a target and establish physical contact with it, often without any assistance from the target itself. This is a demanding proximity operation, and it is only as reliable as the perception system that guides it. Hence, before any physical contact, the perception on-board the servicer satellite must reliably detect the target, estimate its relative pose, and identify suitable grasping points[1]. Among the common structural features of a satellite, the LAR is a distinct structural interface[2][3][4][5] common to most satellites. It is rigid and well-defined, with sharp, easily detectable edges, and has a high loadbearing capacity [6][7][8]. This makes it an ideal target for vision-based detection operations like robotic grappling and berthing in OOS missions, as shown in Fig 1.

Existing classical CV methods mostly rely on handcrafted features such as edges, contours, and geometric shapes[2][5][3]. These features are typically extracted using operators such as Canny, Sobel[9], or Hough Transform (RHT)[10], providing advantages in computational efficiency and interpretability without the need for large training datasets[4][11]. However, due to unfavorable conditions in the space environment, the perception of such structures poses a unique challenge [1]. These include extreme lighting variations, reflectivity of the target’s surface, ineffectiveness during eclipse, inferior resolution[12], and limited processing power[13], which degrade the image features and affect the real-time performance of the system[1].

blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: Recently, deep learning (DL) models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been increasingly applied to spacecraft detection and pose estimation in cooperative and uncooperative scenarios[15][16]. CNNs enable models to automatically learn hierarchical visual features from large datasets, but their heavy training and inference demands pose computational challenges in space, where on-board resources are limited. Overall, the existing literature indicates that LARs are among the most robust geometric primitives for robotic capture on spacecraft, and classical edge-based methods remain widely used because they can reliably extract the ring contours. Across both traditional and learning-based approaches, a common takeaway is that successful satellite pose estimation depends critically on accurate LAR detection. However, existing work has not sufficiently characterized how edge detection performance degrades under changing illumination. Building on this gap, our work introduces a classical approach for reliably detecting the LAR and addressing its limitations, which encouraged this paper to conduct a comparative analysis of classical CV and DL-based methods for LAR detection in robotic OOS operations. The key contributions of this work are:
• The development of a classical geometric detection pipeline for LAR detection based on Canny edge extraction.
• The implementation of a deep learning-based detector for LAR identification through bounding box prediction and classification.
• A comparative evaluation of classical geometric and deep learning–based detection approaches, assessing detection performance and computational efficiency.

For the classical approach we propose a vision-based geometry-driven method to detect the outer and inner ring structures of the LAR using edge detection under different illuminations, angles and distances, while efficiently handling variations in scale, orientation, and noise. Top block of Fig 2 describes the proposed classical pipeline of detection of LAR through each stage of the pipeline, which consists of: (a) image resizing, pre-processing, and detection of ROI, (b) segmentation of the LAR (c) LAR’s feature extraction and ellipse fitting and (d) detection of the LAR.

To reduce the computational cost, we first downscaled the input RGB image by 400% and focused taking a region of interest (ROI). And then the image containing ROI converted into HSV. A silver region mask is applied using low-S and high-V colors space thresholding to isolate metallic silver areas and to increase robustness to gold-foil MLI reflections yellow metallic hues (H) are added to the mask.
A binary mask,

is obtained by combining the silver and yellow masks. The resulting mask is subjected to morphological opening and closing to remove small artifacts while preserving larger curved structures. The masked image is then smoothed using a 5 X 5 Gaussian kernel to suppress noise. Using the detected metallic colors as priors, candidate contours are analyzed based on circularity and approximate size, enabling the estimation of a coarse bounding box around ring-like structures. This bounding box defines a highconfidence ROI. Once the ROI is identified, the algorithm isolates the LAR by focusing on the metallic structures within this cropped region. The resulting bounding box coordinates are retained as the classical method’s ROI output and serve as the basis for detection performance evaluation.

blocks.html: The LAR has reflective properties that differ from the surrounding background, resulting in a sharp change in image brightness and intensity [5]. Hence, edge pixels are extracted to determine the boundary of the ring by applying the Canny operator [17] to the masked image with thresholds derived from local image intensity values. This produces a binary edge map containing potential ring boundaries.

blocks.alt: From the edge map, the contours are ex- tracted using hierarchical tree-structured retrieval

blocks.html: findContours(RETR_TREE) [18] that detects parentchild relationships between the nested structure of the identified contours. This is an important feature for distinguishing inner and outer rings. The contour filtering to eliminate noise and irrelevant features is done using the following criteria:
• It takes at least 5 points to fit an ellipse. So, the number of points should be > 5.
• Minimum area A should be at least ≥0.02% of ROI –
• The number of vertices of the polygon must be ≥6 by Douglas–Peucker polygonal approximation[19] to ensure that only sufficiently smooth, curved shapes are kept.
• Circularity (C) is computed.

Once all criteria are met, shape similarity is assessed using Hu moment invariants [20], integrated into the score as filtered contours are furthermore scored by combining area and circularity. Circularity Score is computed to rank all the ring candidates.
The contour with the highest score is selected as the outer ring candidates.

Ellipses are fitted for the selected inner and outer ring candidates using cv2.fitEllipseAMS[21] using direct leastsquares[22] minimization, solving the conic expression of the ellipse, and then acquiring 5D parameters of the ellipses as:

blocks.html: via eigenvalue decomposition of the design matrix, providing a non-iterative, stable fit robust to noise[22].

Further validation is done on the selected inner and outer rings, by reference ellipses are fitted using the above method and taking geometric parameters: center cxcy, major/minor axes a, b, and rotation angle θ. These parameters serve as reference to quantify detection performance. Key validation metrics are as follows:

blocks.html: We utilize a DL approach for the LAR detection where traditional methods may fail under variable lighting, occlusions, and pose variations. As a lightweight and efficient object detection framework, YOLOv8n[23] is selected for its balance between accuracy, inference speed, and computational efficiency, compared to the other models of the YOLO family [23] [24].

The structure of YOLOv8 is essentially divided into 3 key components: a CSPDarknet-based backbone, a PANet neck, and an anchor-free detection head[24]. Fig 4 shows the YOLOv8n-based LAR detection pipeline.

The dataset for training and evaluation consists of a combination of real-world satellite images that feature the LAR structure. A total of 2214 real images were collected, which included various viewpoints, tumble simulations via arm motion (0–5 deg/s equivalent), different illumination intensities, and partial occlusions. These images were labeled using Label-studio[25] for bounding box coordinates (x, y, width, height) and class ("LAR"). The dataset is divided into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% testing sets, ensuring balanced distribution across angles, illumination conditions, and poses.

To assess the performance of the two approaches, tests were performed on real images taken from the experimental setup illustrated in Fig. 5. The setup consists of a chaser robotic manipulator (UR10) equipped with an end-effector camera, and a second UR10 arm with a satellite mockup that moves on a predefined 6-DoF trajectory. The mockup is a scaled replicate of a real non-cooperative satellite. It includes a 30 cm × 30 cm × 30 cm cube as central body covered in MLI, an attached Launch Adapter Ring and two solar panels.
The models were implemented in Ultralytics 8.4.18 Python- 3.14.3 torch-2.10.0+cpu and executed on a laptop running CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 5800H with Radeon Graphics).

In addition to the validation steps done in Section 2.3, ground truth annotations were used to compute quantitative performance metrics. To enable a like-for-like comparison with the YOLOv8n bounding box output, the coarse bounding box produced by the ROI proposal stage is evaluated against the ground truth bounding box annotations.

blocks.caption: Experimental setup at the Zero-G Lab, University of Luxembourg.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The mAP was computed across multiple IoU thresholds ranging from 0.5 to 0.95 with a step of 0.05. Moreover, the detection rate is evaluated. This evaluation at the bounding box level is also meaningful beyond the comparison itself — the ROI quality directly determines the reliability of the downstream ring detection. Hence, a failed ROI propagates as a detection failure regardless of the ellipse fitting stage. Therefore, the bounding box level comparison also serves as a proxy for overall pipeline reliability, particularly under illumination extremes where the HSV mask degrades.

All runs are initialized from COCO-pretrained YOLOv8n weights provided by Ultralytics[23]. Trained for 100 epochs. We report the COCO-style metrics (precision, recall,and mAP@0.5:0.95) on the testing split. The benchmark expects exactly one label and bounding box per image. We therefore use max_det=1 during inference to enforce a single prediction per frame. Each detection includes the bounding box location and a confidence score indicating the likelihood that the region contains the ring.

Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) method is applied with an IoU threshold of 0.5 and a standard confidence threshold of 0.25 to filter redundant detections. In addition, the inference time per frame is measured to analyze the computational efficiency of the model.

Table 1 presents the quantitative comparison between the evaluated methods using the above mentioned metrics. As shown in the table 1 the YOLO-based detectors demonstrate higher detection accuracy and detection rate, compared to the classical CV approach, however, it is approximately four times more computationally expensive than the classical method. In contrast, the classical Canny-based pipeline provides reliable detection as shown in center image in Fig 6, when the ring edges are clearly visible, but it is more sensitive to noise and lighting changes.

Fig 6 illustrates the qualitative detection results of the methods evaluated under different imaging conditions. The classical approach accurately detects the ring when strong edge features are present, while the YOLO-based detectors demonstrate improved robustness in scenarios with uneven illumination and background clutter.

blocks.html: Although the YOLOv8n model demonstrated significantly higher results, a specific failure mode was identified, when LAR is fully saturated as shown in top three images in Fig 7.

The classical method, as illustrated in Fig. 7, exhibited failures primarily under two challenging illumination conditions: extreme low-light and high-illumination scenarios. Additionally, performance degraded in frames where the LAR was partially occluded, resulting in incomplete or ambiguous boundary information. The Canny operator failed to detect the intensity gradient changes required for reliable edge extraction. As a result, the ROI was sometimes missed entirely as shown in Fig 7 bottom left, while in other cases false ring detections were produced as in the Fig 7 bottom right corner images.

In this paper, we presented a comparative performance analysis of the classical CV methods the DL based method for LAR detection. The results revealed that the YOLOv8n model achieved the highest detection accuracy and detection rate, demonstrating robust and consistent results across all the images, but at the expense of higher computational cost. This makes it less suitable in scenarios with strict processing constraints, such as OOS missions, where computational resources are limited. While the classical method provided a balanced trade-off between computational efficiency and detection accuracy. But overall detection accuracy remained inferior to YOLOv8n. So, future work will focus on improving the computational efficiency of deep learning–based detection methods and exploring hybrid approaches that combine classical techniques with CNN-based detection to balance robustness and computational efficiency.
